facts: Made his first trip outside the Dunwich region the following winter.
Correspondence with several major libraries failed to get him the loan of a book he desperately wanted.
Set out in person to consult the copy at Miskatonic, the nearest to him geographically.
Was shabby, dirty, bearded, and uncouth of dialect.
Was almost eight feet tall.

sources.quote: The following winter brought an event no less strange than Wilbur's first trip outside the Dunwich region.

Almost eight feet tall, and carrying a cheap new valise from Osborn's general store, this dark and goatish gargoyle appeared one day in Arkham in quest of the dreaded volume kept under lock and key at the college library

He had never seen a city before, but had no thought save to find his way to the university grounds; where, indeed, he passed heedlessly by the great white-fanged watchdog that barked with unnatural fury and enmity, and tugged frantically at its stout chain.

Wilbur had with him the priceless but imperfect copy of Dr. Dee's English version which his grandfather had bequeathed him, and upon receiving access to the Latin copy he at once began to collate the two texts with the aim of discovering a certain passage which would have come on the 751st page of his own defective volume.
He was looking, he had to admit, for a kind of formula or incantation containing the frightful name Yog-Sothoth
Presently Wilbur raised his head and began speaking in that strange, resonant fashion which hinted at sound-producing organs unlike the run of mankind's.
"Wal, all right, ef ye feel that way abaout it. Maybe Harvard wun't be so fussy as yew be." And without saying more he rose and strode out of the building, stooping at each doorway.
Armitage heard the savage yelping of the great watchdog, and studied Whateley's gorilla-like lope as he crossed the bit of campus visible from the window.
He had heard, meanwhile, of Whateley's grotesque trip to Cambridge, and of his frantic efforts to borrow or copy from the Necronomicon at the Widener Library.
Wilbur had been shockingly nervous at Cambridge; anxious for the book, yet almost equally anxious to get home again, as if he feared the results of being away long.

name: Henry Armitage
facts: Was the librarian at Miskatonic, holding degrees A.M. Miskatonic, Ph.D. Princeton, Litt.D. Johns Hopkins.
Had once called at the Whateley farm.
Politely plied Wilbur with questions.
Looked involuntarily over Wilbur's shoulder at the open Necronomicon pages.
Mentally translated the Latin text he read.
Associated the text with what he had heard of Dunwich and Wilbur's dim, hideous aura.
Felt a wave of fright as tangible as a draft of the tomb's cold clamminess.
Refused to let Wilbur take the Necronomicon home.
Heard the savage yelping of the watchdog as Wilbur left.
Recalled wild tales, old Sunday stories in the Advertiser, and lore from Dunwich rustics.
Locked away the Necronomicon with a shudder of disgust.
Noticed the room reeked with an unholy stench, the same odor that had sickened him at the Whateley farmhouse less than three years before.
Muttered aloud questioning what or who was Wilbur Whateley's father.
Set about collecting all possible data on Wilbur Whateley and the presences around Dunwich.
Got in communication with Dr. Houghton of Aylesbury.
Made a visit to Dunwich Village that failed to bring out much new information.
Made a close survey of the parts of the Necronomicon Wilbur had sought.
Had talks with students of archaic lore in Boston and wrote letters to others elsewhere.
Felt growing amazement passing into a state of acute spiritual fear.
Issued warnings to all librarians having charge of the Necronomicon, including at Widener Library.
Was among those who witnessed the monstrous prologue of the Dunwich horror in 1928.

sources.quote: the same erudite Henry Armitage (A. M. Miskatonic, Ph. D. Princeton, Litt. D. Johns Hopkins) who had once called at the farm, and who now politely plied him with questions.
As he copied the formula he finally chose, Dr. Armitage looked involuntarily over his shoulder at the open pages

Dr. Armitage, associating what he was reading with what he had heard of Dunwich and its brooding presences, and of Wilbur Whateley and his dim, hideous aura that stretched from a dubious birth to a cloud of probable matricide, felt a wave of fright as tangible as a draft of the tomb's cold clamminess.
There was too much responsibility in giving such a being the key to such blasphemous outer spheres.
He locked away the Necronomicon with a shudder of disgust, but the room still reeked with an unholy and unidentifiable stench.
Yes—the odor was the same as that which had sickened him at the Whateley farmhouse less than three years before.
"Inbreeding?" Armitage muttered half aloud to himself.
During the ensuing weeks Dr. Armitage set about to collect all possible data on Wilbur Whateley and the formless presences around Dunwich.
He got in communication with Dr. Houghton of Aylesbury, who had attended Old Whateley in his last illness, and found much to ponder over in the grandfather's last words as quoted by the physician.
Dr. Armitage was among those who witnessed its monstrous prologue.
Those efforts had been in vain, since Armitage had issued warnings of the keenest intensity to all librarians having charge of the dreaded volume.

Wilbur sought a formula or incantation containing this name.

name: The Old Ones
facts: Were, are, and shall be, existing not in the spaces we know but between them.
Walk serene and primal, undimensioned and unseen to us.
Broke through of old and shall break through again where Yog-Sothoth knows.
Have trod earth's fields and still tread them, though no one can behold them as they tread.
Can sometimes be known by men through their smell, but their semblance cannot be known save through the features of beings they have begotten on mankind.
Walk unseen and foul in lonely places where certain Words have been spoken and Rites howled through at their Seasons.
Bend the forest and crush the city, yet may not be beheld doing so.
Have their seal engraven on stones in the ice desert of the South and the sunken isles of Ocean.
Great Cthulhu is said to be their cousin, able to spy them only dimly.
Man rules now where they ruled once, and they shall soon rule again where man rules now.
